title: Computing joint, marginal, and conditional probabilities from a contingency table
scenario_markdown:
A digital marketing team analyzes conversion responses from an email promotional campaign sent to $n = 500$ registered retail customers. Customers are cross-classified by age category ($A_1$: Under 30 years old; $A_2$: 30 years or older) and purchase behavior ($B$: Made a purchase; $B^c$: Did not make a purchase):

| Age Group | Purchased ($B$) | Did Not Purchase ($B^c$) | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Under 30 ($A_1$)** | $60$ | $140$ | $200$ |
| **30 or Older ($A_2$)** | $120$ | $180$ | $300$ |
| **Total** | $180$ | $320$ | $500$ |

Calculate the relevant probabilities, distinguish joint from marginal and conditional outcomes, and evaluate whether purchase behavior is independent of age category.

parameters.objective: Compute marginal, joint, and conditional probabilities from a two-way contingency table and test for statistical independence

assumptions: Total sample size is n = 500 recipients
Joint probability P(A and B) = count(A and B) / n
Conditional probability P(B | A) = count(A and B) / total(A)
source_refs: Course Module 1: Descriptive Measures & Basic Probability

approval.notes: Reviewed probability derivation: n = 500. Marginal P(B) = 180/500 = 0.360. Joint P(A1 and B) = 60/500 = 0.120. Conditional P(B | A1) = 60/200 = 0.300. P(B | A2) = 120/300 = 0.400. Because P(B | A1) = 0.300 != P(B) = 0.360, purchase is dependent on age (older cohort converts at 40% vs younger at 30%).

stages.prompt_markdown: What is the **joint probability** that a randomly selected recipient is under 30 years old AND made a purchase, $P(A_1 \cap B)$?

options.text_markdown: **$P(A_1 \cap B) = \frac{60}{500} = 0.120$ ($12.0\%$)**: The count in the intersection cell divided by the grand total.
**$P(B) = \frac{180}{500} = 0.360$ ($36.0\%$)**: The total count of all purchasers divided by the grand total.
options.hint_markdown: This is the marginal probability of making a purchase across all age groups; joint probability requires satisfying both conditions simultaneously ($60/500$).

options.text_markdown: **$P(B \mid A_1) = \frac{60}{200} = 0.300$ ($30.0\%$)**: The count of purchasers under 30 divided by the row total.
options.hint_markdown: Dividing by the row total $200$ gives conditional probability; joint probability divides by the grand total $500$.

stages.explanation_markdown: A **joint probability** $P(A_1 \cap B)$ is the probability that two events occur simultaneously. From the table, the intersection cell of 'Under 30' and 'Purchased' contains $60$ recipients out of the grand total of $500$, giving $P(A_1 \cap B) = \frac{60}{500} = 0.120$ ($12.0\%$).

stages.prompt_markdown: Given that a customer is under 30 years old ($A_1$), what is the **conditional probability** that they made a purchase, $P(B \mid A_1)$?

options.text_markdown: **$P(B \mid A_1) = \frac{60}{200} = 0.300$ ($30.0\%$)**: The sample space is restricted to the $200$ recipients in the 'Under 30' row.
**$P(A_1 \mid B) = \frac{60}{180} \approx 0.333$ ($33.3\%$)**: Dividing by the column total of purchasers.
options.hint_markdown: The condition is that the customer is under 30 ($A_1$), so the denominator must be the row total $200$, not the purchaser column total $180$.

options.text_markdown: **$P(A_1 \cap B) = \frac{60}{500} = 0.120$ ($12.0\%$)**: Dividing by the grand total of $500$.
options.hint_markdown: Conditional probability conditions on the subset: $P(B \mid A_1) = \frac{P(A_1 \cap B)}{P(A_1)} = \frac{60}{200} = 0.300$.

stages.explanation_markdown: By the definition of **conditional probability**, $P(B \mid A_1) = \frac{P(A_1 \cap B)}{P(A_1)} = \frac{60 / 500}{200 / 500} = \frac{60}{200} = 0.300$ ($30.0\%$). The given condition 'Under 30' restricts the effective sample space to the row of $200$ younger customers.

stages.prompt_markdown: Is the purchase decision ($B$) statistically **independent** of whether the customer is under 30 ($A_1$)?

options.text_markdown: **No, the events are dependent**: Because $P(B \mid A_1) = 0.300 \ne P(B) = 0.360$ (and $P(B \mid A_2) = \frac{120}{300} = 0.400$), knowing a customer's age category alters the probability that they will make a purchase.
**Yes, the events are independent**: Because the rows sum to $500$, all categories in a contingency table are automatically independent.
options.hint_markdown: Rows and columns always sum to grand totals; independence requires conditional probabilities to equal overall marginal probabilities.

options.text_markdown: **Yes, the events are independent**: Because $P(A_1 \cap B) = 0.120 > 0$, any positive intersection implies statistical independence.
options.hint_markdown: Independence requires $P(A_1 \cap B) = P(A_1) \times P(B)$; here $0.120 \ne 0.40 \times 0.36 = 0.144$.

stages.explanation_markdown: Two events are independent if and only if $P(B \mid A_1) = P(B)$ (or equivalently $P(A_1 \cap B) = P(A_1) P(B)$). Here, the overall marginal purchase rate is $P(B) = \frac{180}{500} = 0.360$. For younger customers, the conversion rate is only $P(B \mid A_1) = 0.300$, whereas for older customers it is $P(B \mid A_2) = \frac{120}{300} = 0.400$. Because $0.300 \ne 0.360 \ne 0.400$, **purchase behavior and age category are statistically dependent** (older recipients convert at a higher rate).
